codeagent -- the server side of M2C (the `m2c` terminal client's brain).

Named `codeagent`, not `m2c`, so it can never clash with the top-level `m2c/`
client package when both sit in one dev environment (build plan O5).

Patch S04 creates this package with the device socket (ws.py, connections.py).
Later patches add modules beside them (the model adapter, the run manager, the
tool broker); this file stays empty of imports on purpose, so importing a
sibling never drags in the socket or its dependencies.

codeagent/adapters/ -- model adapters for the M2C server (patch S05).

One module per provider family, all speaking the provider-neutral interface
defined in codeagent/model_adapter.py:

    openai_compat.py   OpenAI-compatible chat completions with native tool use
                       (Groq, Mistral, Gemini's OpenAI layer, the Hugging Face
                       router, OpenRouter, or any other base URL). First adapter,
                       build plan decision D3. An Anthropic adapter is second and
                       a Gemini-native one third; they are separate patches.
    toolcalls.py       Tolerant tool-call parsing, ported from MiniLocker
                       (decision D12). Pure functions, no network.

Nothing is imported here on purpose. `import codeagent.adapters.toolcalls`
must stay cheap and must not drag in the OpenAI SDK, `utils.llm_client` (and
through it Redis, the database layer and every provider SDK) or any other
heavy module; import the module you need explicitly.

NAMESPACE NOTE. This patch deliberately does not create backend/codeagent/
__init__.py: patch S04 creates it in parallel. Until both are applied
`codeagent` is a plain namespace package, which is enough for
`from codeagent.adapters import toolcalls` and for the tests under
backend/tests/unit/test_codeagent_*.py to import it. Once S04's file exists
it becomes a regular package and nothing here changes.

codeagent/adapters/openai_compat.py -- OpenAI-compatible chat completions with native tool use (patch S05,
decision D3). Streams `text_delta`, `tool_call` and `usage` events (codeagent/model_adapter.py).

WHICH PROVIDERS. Anything that speaks OpenAI's /chat/completions with `tools` and `stream=True`: Groq, Mistral,
Gemini's OpenAI layer, the Hugging Face router, OpenRouter, or any other base URL. These are exactly the providers
utils/llm_client.py already has client factories for, and this adapter reuses those (see KEY SELECTION).

HOW A CALL RUNS
  * The request goes out with `stream=True` and `stream_options={"include_usage": True}`; if an SDK version rejects
    the second kwarg (TypeError) it is retried without, and usage then comes from wherever the provider puts it or
    is reported as unreported (never an error: metering fails open).
  * The provider SDKs here are synchronous. A daemon worker thread iterates the SDK stream and hands chunks to the
    event loop through an asyncio.Queue (the same bridge utils/llm_client.py's _walk_chain_once_stream uses, but one
    dedicated thread per stream instead of the shared executor, so a long stream can never starve other work and
    cannot keep the interpreter alive at shutdown). All parsing happens on the loop side, single-threaded.
  * Closing the async generator, or cancelling the task that iterates it, sets a stop flag and closes the HTTP
    stream; the worker exits. That is how a run's `cancel` reaches the provider.

Tolerant tool-call handling, for models that do not honour the OpenAI tool-calling contract to the letter.

Three things go wrong in practice, and this module fixes each one:

  * the structured call is *almost* right: arguments wrapped in a code fence, a trailing comma, single
    quotes, a `functions.` prefix on the name, or an object where a JSON string belongs;
  * the provider rejects a malformed call with HTTP 400 `tool_use_failed` but hands back what the model
    wrote (`failed_generation`), and that text is usually a perfectly clear call in another syntax;
  * the model writes the call as *text* in its own native syntax (Hermes `<tool_call>`, Llama `<function=..>`,
    Kimi `<|tool_call_begin|>`, gpt-oss "harmony", ReAct, or bare JSON) instead of using the structured field.

Everything here is pure (no network, no Docker), so it is cheap to test exhaustively.

Rules that keep this safe. Model output is untrusted, and parsing free text for "a tool call" is exactly the
place where a prompt injection could be promoted into an action, so the parser is conservative:

  1. Only text that *consists of* tool-call markup counts. Prose that merely quotes some JSON (a summary of a
     hostile page, say) is not a call. Protocol-token formats tolerate a short preamble; free-form JSON and
     ReAct do not. The one relaxation is `failed_generation`, where the provider has already decided the text
     was an attempted call.
  2. Reasoning blocks (`<think>...</think>`) are removed

codeagent/broker.py -- S09: the server tool broker.

The agent loop (S07) decides the model wants a tool run. The tool runs on the user's DEVICE,
under the device's own policy. The broker is the one place on the server that carries that
exchange: it proposes the call to the connected device, waits for the answer, and turns
whatever happens (a result, a denial, silence, a lost connection, a cancel) into exactly one
outcome for the loop and exactly one `tool_finished` event for the device's stream.

    loop (S07)  --propose(...)-->  broker  --tool_proposed-->  emit  -->  device
                <--ToolOutcome---          <--tool_result / approval / tool_stream--  (router, S14)

THE CALL LIFECYCLE (protocol/README.md sections 2, 3 and 5)
-----------------------------------------------------------
    1. propose(): the broker registers the call and emits `tool_proposed` {call_id, tool,
       input, risk}: a STREAM message, so it carries a seq, which the emitter assigns.
    2. The device's policy decides. It answers with `approval` {call_id, decision, scope} when
       a decision was made, and with `tool_result` {call_id, ok, output, truncated, trust, ...}
       if it ran the tool. A DENIED call gets an approval with decision `deny` and NO
       tool_result: the broker finishes it at once instead of waiting for a timeout.
    3. The call ends exactly once, with one `run_event tool_finished` {call_id, tool, status,
       duration_ms}. status is one of:

           ok

codeagent/buffer.py -- S06 (part b): the ephemeral, encrypted run buffer.

While a run is active the server must keep two things so the loop can call the model
and so a device that drops can come back (build plan section O1, "Server, ephemeral
content"):

  * the CONVERSATION: the run's state (profile, mode, instructions, ...) and every
    history item, so the next model call can be built and prompt-cache prefixes stay
    stable;
  * the REPLAY EVENTS: every stream message (run_event, tool_proposed, budget_warning)
    the server sent to the device, stored VERBATIM, so run.resume{last_seq} can
    re-deliver everything after last_seq with the same id and seq (protocol/README.md
    section 5). They carry reply text and tool output, so they are content too.

Both live ONLY here: in Redis, through the existing Upstash client (memory.bus.redis),
encrypted with AES-GCM, expiring, and deleted when the run ends. Never Postgres, never a
log line. runs.py (S06 part a) is the content-free record of the same run; this module is
the content half and never touches that table.

codeagent/context.py -- Patch S08: the context assembler v0 (budgets, cache-stable order, mechanical compaction).

WHAT THIS IS. `BudgetedContextAssembler` is the object the agent loop (loop.py, S07) is given in place of
prompts.DefaultContextAssembler. It keeps the same interface, `assemble(state, items, tools, mode) ->
AssembledContext`, synchronous, and adds what the default says it leaves out (prompts.py, "NOT HERE"): a size

codeagent/router.py -- S14 (part a): the message router.

S04's socket (ws.py) authenticates and validates, then hands every message other than
`ping` to ONE installed MessageHandler (ws.set_message_handler). This module is that
handler. It does one thing: look at the message's type `t` and give the message to the
function registered for it. What those functions do (start a run, queue a turn, cancel,
resume, pause on disconnect) is S14c-e's; how their events reach the device is S14b's.

    ws.py (S04)        authenticated, validated, rate-limited connection
    router.py (here)   dispatch by message type; contain a handler's mistakes
    emitter.py         S14b: numbered, stored, delivered server events
    run_handlers.py    S14c-e: the handlers that are registered here
    run_manager.py     S06: start, resume, pause, end, cancel

THE RULES
---------
* Dispatch is by `msg["t"]`, nothing else. The router never reads a payload: it cannot
  leak what it does not look at, and it cannot get a payload wrong.
* A message type with no registered handler is answered with the protocol error
  `internal`, with the message's id as ref_id and a fixed text (MSG_NO_HANDLER). Never
